note: Held areas are approximate. There was no continuous front: ground is drawn as held where an army or garrison controlled it, Sherman's paths through Georgia and the Carolinas are shown as Union-held after his armies passed, and raids and guerrilla country are not shown.

chapters.title: Secession and Fort Sumter
chapters.text: After Abraham Lincoln, who opposed the spread of slavery, won the election of 1860, seven Deep South states seceded, and in February 1861 they formed the Confederate States of America at Montgomery, Alabama. Confederate batteries bombarded Fort Sumter in Charleston harbour on 12 April and it surrendered the next day. When Lincoln called for troops to put down the rebellion, Virginia, Arkansas, North Carolina and Tennessee also left the Union, between April and June.

chapters.title: Bull Run and western Virginia
arrows: Confederate reinforcements by rail from the Shenandoah Valley
chapters.text: Union troops crossed the Potomac and occupied Alexandria on 24 May, while General George McClellan drove the Confederates out of north-western Virginia in June and July, where many people opposed secession. Pressed for a quick march on Richmond, General Irvin McDowell attacked the Confederates at Manassas on 21 July. Reinforcements arriving by train turned the First Battle of Bull Run into a Union rout, and both sides saw that the war would be long.

chapters.title: The rivers of the West, 1862
arrows: Grant takes Forts Henry and Donelson
Pope takes New Madrid and Island No. 10
chapters.text: In February Ulysses S. Grant's army and river gunboats took Fort Henry and Fort Donelson, forcing the Confederates out of Kentucky and Nashville. A Confederate surprise attack at Shiloh on 6 April was beaten back at great cost, and the Union went on to take Corinth on 30 May and Memphis on 6 June. In late April a Union fleet under David Farragut ran past the forts below New Orleans and captured the South's largest city, leaving only the stretch around Vicksburg in Confederate hands.

chapters.title: The Peninsula campaign
chapters.text: McClellan shipped his army to Fort Monroe and advanced slowly up the peninsula between the York and James rivers, taking Yorktown in early May while Norfolk fell on 10 May. By late May his troops could see the church spires of Richmond. Robert E. Lee, who took command of the Confederate army on 1 June, struck back in the Seven Days Battles (25 June – 1 July) and drove McClellan back to the James River.

chapters.title: Second Bull Run and Antietam
chapters.text: Lee turned north, outmanoeuvred John Pope's army and defeated it at the Second Battle of Bull Run (28–30 August), clearing northern Virginia of Union troops. He then invaded Maryland, where Stonewall Jackson captured the Union garrison at Harpers Ferry on 15 September. On 17 September McClellan attacked Lee along Antietam Creek near Sharpsburg in the bloodiest single day of the war; Lee retreated into Virginia, and on 22 September Lincoln issued the preliminary Emancipation Proclamation.

chapters.title: Fredericksburg and Chancellorsville
arrows: Burnside crosses the Rappahannock at Fredericksburg
chapters.text: The Union army under Ambrose Burnside crossed the Rappahannock and assaulted Lee's lines behind Fredericksburg on 13 December 1862, and was thrown back with heavy losses. In late April 1863 Joseph Hooker marched round Lee's flank to Chancellorsville, but Lee divided his smaller army and Jackson's flank attack on 2 May routed the Union right. Hooker retreated across the river on 6 May; Jackson had been mortally wounded by his own men.

chapters.title: Vicksburg
arrows: Grant marches down the west bank
Grant crosses at Bruinsburg and drives on Jackson
chapters.text: Grant marched his army down the Louisiana side of the Mississippi, crossed below Vicksburg on 30 April and struck inland, taking Jackson on 14 May before turning west. After winning at Champion Hill he besieged Vicksburg from 18 May. The starving garrison surrendered on 4 July, and Port Hudson followed on 9 July, giving the Union the whole Mississippi and cutting off Texas, Arkansas and western Louisiana from the rest of the Confederacy.

chapters.title: Gettysburg
arrows: The Union army concentrates at Gettysburg
chapters.text: In June Lee marched north again, cleared the Shenandoah Valley at Winchester and spread into Pennsylvania, reaching Chambersburg, Carlisle and York. The two armies met at Gettysburg on 1 July; after three days of fighting, ending with the failed Confederate assault known as Pickett's Charge, Lee retreated. His army recrossed the Potomac on 13–14 July; it never again invaded the North in force.

chapters.title: Tullahoma, Chickamauga and Chattanooga
chapters.text: William Rosecrans manoeuvred the Confederates out of Middle Tennessee in the Tullahoma campaign (24 June – 3 July) and took Chattanooga on 9 September, while Ambrose Burnside occupied Knoxville. Braxton Bragg's army counter-attacked at Chickamauga (19–20 September), the largest Confederate victory in the West, and besieged the Union army in Chattanooga. Grant arrived, opened a supply line and on 25 November stormed Missionary Ridge, driving Bragg into Georgia.

chapters.title: The Overland campaign and Petersburg
arrows: Grant crosses the Rapidan: the Wilderness and Spotsylvania
On to the North Anna and Cold Harbor
chapters.text: Grant, now general-in-chief, crossed the Rapidan on 4 May 1864 and fought Lee in the Wilderness, at Spotsylvania and at Cold Harbor, losing heavily but moving south each time. In June he crossed the James and began a siege of Petersburg, the rail hub that fed Richmond, which lasted nine months. Jubal Early's Confederates raided to the outskirts of Washington in July, but Philip Sheridan defeated them in the Shenandoah Valley in September and October.

chapters.title: Atlanta and the March to the Sea
chapters.text: William T. Sherman advanced from Chattanooga in May 1864, flanking Joseph Johnston's army back towards Atlanta, which fell on 2 September and helped Lincoln win re-election. In mid-November Sherman burned much of Atlanta's railways and industry and marched about 60,000 men across Georgia towards the coast, living off the land and destroying railways and farms along a path some 60 miles wide. Savannah fell on 21 December.

chapters.title: The Carolinas and Appomattox
chapters.text: Sherman turned north through the Carolinas, taking Columbia on 17 February as Charleston was abandoned, while Union troops took Wilmington. On 2 April Grant broke through at Petersburg; Richmond fell the next day, and Lee surrendered his army at Appomattox Court House on 9 April. Joseph Johnston surrendered in North Carolina on 26 April, and the last major Confederate force west of the Mississippi gave up on 26 May; Lincoln had been assassinated on 14 April.
